metadata.description: Annual meteor shower calendar with peak dates and viewing information
metadata.note: Dates may vary slightly year to year; peak times are approximate

meteorShowers.name: Quadrantids
meteorShowers.description: One of the best annual meteor showers with a sharp peak lasting only a few hours. Best viewed from the Northern Hemisphere.
meteorShowers.viewingTips: The radiant rises after midnight, making the early morning hours best for viewing.

meteorShowers.name: Lyrids
meteorShowers.description: One of the oldest known meteor showers, observed for over 2,700 years. Known for occasional bright fireballs.
meteorShowers.viewingTips: Best viewed after midnight when the radiant is highest in the sky.

meteorShowers.name: Eta Aquariids
meteorShowers.description: Produced by debris from Halley's Comet. Best viewed from southern latitudes but visible worldwide.
meteorShowers.viewingTips: Best viewing is in the pre-dawn hours. The radiant is low for Northern Hemisphere observers.

meteorShowers.name: Southern Delta Aquariids
meteorShowers.description: A steady shower best viewed from southern latitudes. Often overlaps with the early Perseids.
meteorShowers.viewingTips: The radiant is best positioned around 2-3 AM local time.

meteorShowers.name: Perseids
meteorShowers.description: The most popular meteor shower due to its reliability and warm summer viewing conditions. Known for producing bright fireballs.
meteorShowers.viewingTips: Best after midnight when Perseus is high in the northeastern sky. Can see meteors all night.

meteorShowers.name: Orionids
meteorShowers.description: Second shower from Halley's Comet debris. Known for fast meteors and occasional fireballs.
meteorShowers.viewingTips: Best after midnight when Orion rises. The radiant is highest around dawn.

meteorShowers.name: Southern Taurids
meteorShowers.description: A long-running shower known for slow, bright fireballs rather than high rates.
meteorShowers.viewingTips: Visible all night when Taurus is above the horizon.

meteorShowers.name: Northern Taurids
meteorShowers.description: Sister shower to the Southern Taurids, also known for slow, bright fireballs.
meteorShowers.viewingTips: Visible most of the night. Both Taurid showers can produce impressive fireballs.

meteorShowers.name: Leonids
meteorShowers.description: Famous for producing meteor storms approximately every 33 years. Normally modest but can be spectacular.
meteorShowers.viewingTips: Best after midnight when Leo rises. The radiant is highest just before dawn.

meteorShowers.name: Geminids
meteorShowers.description: Considered the best annual meteor shower. Produces bright, colorful meteors with a high rate.
meteorShowers.viewingTips: Visible all night, with the radiant rising in the early evening. Best after 9 PM.

meteorShowers.name: Ursids
meteorShowers.description: A modest shower occurring near the winter solstice. The circumpolar radiant means it's visible all night for northern observers.
meteorShowers.viewingTips: Best for Northern Hemisphere observers. The radiant never sets, so viewing is possible all night.

meteorShowers.name: Alpha Centaurids
meteorShowers.description: A Southern Hemisphere shower with occasional bright meteors.
meteorShowers.viewingTips: Only visible from southern latitudes. Best viewed in the early morning hours.

meteorShowers.name: Pi Puppids
meteorShowers.description: A variable Southern Hemisphere shower with slow-moving meteors.
meteorShowers.viewingTips: Best viewed from southern latitudes in the evening and early morning.

meteorShowers.name: Alpha Capricornids
meteorShowers.description: Known for producing bright, slow fireballs. Low rates but impressive meteors.
meteorShowers.viewingTips: Best after midnight when the radiant is highest. Overlaps with the Delta Aquariids.

meteorShowers.name: Kappa Cygnids
meteorShowers.description: A minor shower notable for slow, bright meteors.
meteorShowers.viewingTips: Best viewed in the Northern Hemisphere when Cygnus is high overhead.

meteorShowers.name: Draconids
meteorShowers.description: A variable shower that can produce outbursts when Earth passes through denser debris streams.
meteorShowers.viewingTips: Unlike most showers, best viewed in the evening rather than after midnight.

meteorShowers.name: Phoenicids
meteorShowers.description: A Southern Hemisphere shower with slow-moving meteors.
meteorShowers.viewingTips: Only visible from southern latitudes. Best viewed in the early evening.

meteorShowers.name: Sigma Hydrids
meteorShowers.description: A minor shower that peaks near the Geminids.
meteorShowers.viewingTips: Best viewed after midnight. Often overlooked due to the concurrent Geminids.

meteorShowers.name: December Monocerotids
meteorShowers.description: A minor December shower with occasional bright meteors.
meteorShowers.viewingTips: Best viewed after midnight when Monoceros is high in the sky.

meteorShowers.name: Puppid-Velids
meteorShowers.description: A Southern Hemisphere shower complex with multiple radiants.
meteorShowers.viewingTips: Best viewed from southern latitudes during the pre-dawn hours.
